title: Contextual Causal Bayesian Optimisation
claim: Each iteration selects among candidate sub-policies by an upper-confidence score, then acts on the chosen one and updates its statistics.
layout: 3 colored stages, left-to-right, braces with labels beneath
description: A horizontal flow diagram for one iteration t of the algorithm. At far left is a blue box listing the 1st through m-th POMPS candidates. Each is scored as S_i(n_i), an empirical mean plus a bonus that shrinks with the pull count, and a vertical ellipsis separates the first and last entries. An arrow leads to a blue ellipse that picks i_t by argmax. Another arrow enters a green box with three stacked steps: observe the context, choose x_t by maximising a UCB, then record x_t and observe y_t. A final arrow leads to a yellow box that updates the Gaussian process, increments the count n_{i_t}, and recomputes the UCB. Curly braces under the boxes label them POMPS Selection, Action Selection and Update. A small 'At iteration t' tag sits at top left. The eye goes first to the blue and green boxes.
caption: At each iteration t, we select a POMPS using the running average of the UCB evaluated at the points xt and ct, plus an exploration term ρi(ni)/√ni, where ni is the number of times POMPS i has been chosen so far. We then implement the intervention Xit, observe the target yt under this intervention, and update the parameters of the algorithm. For more details please see Algorithm 2.
abstract: We introduce a unified framework for contextual and causal Bayesian optimisation, which aims to design intervention policies maximising the expectation of a target variable. Our approach leverages both observed contextual information and known causal graph structures to guide the search. Within this framework, we propose a novel algorithm that jointly optimises over policies and the sets of variables on which these policies are defined. This thereby extends and unifies two previously distinct approaches: Causal Bayesian Optimisation and Contextual Bayesian Optimisation, while also addressing their limitations in scenarios that yield suboptimal results. We derive worst-case and instance-dependent high-probability regret bounds for our algorithm. We report experimental results across diverse environments, corroborating that our approach achieves sublinear regret and reduces sample complexity in high-dimensional settings.
